title: How were Pompeii’s body casts made?
hook: They aren’t bodies turned to stone: they’re the hollows the bodies left in the ash, filled with plaster.
summary: In the 1860s Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into the hollows left in the ash by decayed bodies; in 2024, DNA showed that several stories told about them were assumptions.
cardText: The bodies decayed inside the hardened ash and left hollows in their shape. In the 1860s, the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli filled those hollows with liquid plaster.

cardBlocks.text: Picture an empty cake mould. At Pompeii, a thick layer of ash covered the victims and hardened around them. Over time the bodies decayed, leaving hollows in their exact shape. In the 1860s, the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli poured liquid plaster into those spaces. The casts show even the folds of clothing and the straps of sandals.

Fragments of bone stayed inside the plaster. In 2024, a team extracted DNA from 14 casts and found that some stories repeated for generations don’t hold up. The adult with a gold bracelet holding a child, always described as a mother and her child, was a man unrelated to the child.
The casts are plaster filling the space the bodies left; DNA showed that some of their stories were modern assumptions.

deepDiveBlocks.text: Fiorelli directed the Pompeii excavations from 1863 to 1875. Instead of clearing the streets first and digging houses up from the ground floor, he had houses uncovered from the top down, which preserved finds better. The plaster technique also recreated plants, which left hollows in the ash just as people did.

The study, published in November 2024 in the journal Current Biology, brought together archaeologists and geneticists from the University of Florence, Harvard and the Max Planck Institute for Evolutionary Anthropology. They looked at 14 of the 86 casts being restored. Besides the bracelet case, a pair seen as two sisters, or mother and daughter, included at least one male. A group of four taken for parents and children turned out to be unrelated. The DNA also showed that many of the people descended mainly from recent immigrants from the eastern Mediterranean.

The researchers add a warning of their own. Harvard geneticist David Reich says the results shouldn’t become the seed of new invented narratives, but a reminder of the risk of projecting today’s ideas about gender and family onto past societies. Anthropologist David Caramelli, of Florence, puts it simply: stories built on thin evidence tend to mirror the worldview of the people telling them.

claims.text: A thick layer of volcanic ash covered Pompeii’s victims and preserved their forms.

support.excerpt: When a volcanic eruption buried the Roman city of Pompeii nearly 2,000 years ago, a thick layer of volcanic ash encased the bodies, preserving their forms.

claims.text: The bodies decayed inside the ash and left hollows in their shape; in the 1860s Giuseppe Fiorelli poured liquid plaster into them.

support.excerpt: In the 1860s a pioneering Italian archaeologist at Pompeii, Giuseppe Fiorelli, poured liquid plaster into the cavities in the solidified ash created by the decomposing flesh, creating perfect casts of Pompeii’s victims at the moment of their deaths—down to the folds in their togas, the straps of their sandals, their agonized facial expressions.

he developed the use of plaster casts to recreate the forms of plants and human bodies that had been covered by the volcanic ash, and had then left a hole - shaped in the form of the plant or person - in that ash after putrefaction.
